Q: `PostAsJsonAsync` returns 500 Internal Server Error from Azure Functions while Postman and `PostAsync` with `StringContent` succeed A:

PostAsJsonAsync is really an extension method that uses JsonContent instead of StringContent. Problem might be that JsonContent is using chunked encoding by default which was documented as an issue for Azure Logic Apps HTTP triggers. More info in this this github issue:

I have to say the Azure Logic App HTTP trigger doesn't support "chunked encoding". In Handle large messages with chunking in Azure Logic Apps doc, it says:

Logic App triggers don't support chunking because of the increased overhead of exchanging multiple messages.

I was trying to POST a message to Azure Logic App with a HTTP trigger. It because HttpClient's PostAsJsonAsync ONLY support chunked encoding by default. I know what @davidfowl said not recommend buffering for large JSON payloads, but most of the payload to the Azure Logic App are really small. I think it should have an straightforward option to use PostAsJsonAsync without chunked encoding.

You can test the work-around mentioned there to test if that's indeed the problem for Azure Functions HTTP trigger as well.

var content = JsonContent.Create<T>(json);
await content.LoadIntoBufferAsync();
var response = await httpClient.PostAsync(url, content);

If it helps, you can turn the code easily in a convenient extension method similar to PostAsJsonAsync.

Q: Why do my results different following along the tiny asm example? A:

I reached the same size removing the same two types of bloat: alignment padding and metadata.

nasm -f elf32 tiny.asm
gcc -m32 -s -no-pie -nostdlib -Wl,-N -Wl,--build-id=none tiny.o -o tiny_peter32
/usr/bin/x86_64-linux-gnu-ld.bfd: warning: tiny_peter32 has a LOAD segment with RWX permissions

Obtained size:
-rwxrwxr-x 1 peter john 248 May 4 00:01 tiny_peter32
-rwxrwxr-x 1 peter john 248 May 4 00:00 tiny_cordes32 (main/first OP answer replication, equivalent to: “a.out” from “foo.asm”)

Alignment / Alignment+Permissions: 
-Wl,-N (OMAGIC) is more aggressive. It disables the 4KB page alignment and makes the code section writable (-Wl,--nmagic (NMAGIC) disables alignment but keeps the code read-only).
-s prevents the linker from writing symbol tables (equivalent to post command-line strip).
--build-id=none removes the .note.gnu.build-id section.


I tried many options that were about to work, but I was getting all the time the same error: /usr/bin/x86_64-linux-gnu-ld.bfd: tiny_peter32: error: PHDR segment not covered by LOAD segment /usr/bin/x86_64-linux-gnu-ld.bfd: warning: tiny_peter32 has a LOAD segment with RWX permissions collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

All changed when adding -no-pie that removes the structures required for that kind of executable.

Q: GNU assembler override size of immediate operand A:

For answer to that question depends on your needs,
Because in your first example you specified only 1 byte as immediate value, which is correct!
However, from another perspective, there’s an advantage:
- the remaining 3 bytes will be processed by AND opcode and they will be zeroed effectively with one instruction! Unlike second example who process only 8-bit and leaves unchanged other bits. If you still need to zero after all, i'd recommended using XOR to clear registers and then continue with your needs.
- cpu loves operate 32bit/64bit/extended registers as opposed to 8 or 16 bit, for example:
1. 8bit instruction with followed operands: sil/dil/bpl/spl needs an additional opcode prefix: 41 (RAX.WB) for correctly interpretation. Also you can't use AH/BH/CH/DH operands with previously mentioned registers, will be occurred UD / at best scenario: exception from GNU Assembler Compiler.
2. mostly 16-bit instructions need an additional 66 byte prefix (Operand-size override prefix) for operate only 16bit register part. For example a cliche: addw $60, %cx. *Default Compiler as you may have noticed wouldn't optimize such things.
*
Good luck. dcgvm.

Q: Discord.js - JSON Parsing? A:

You can get an array of the object values with Object.values()

let gamenames = Object.values(games)

Then,you can loop through the array elements to add them to a string.

let myString = "List: \n"
gamenames.forEach((val) => {
 myString += `• ${val} \n`
})

myString is now equal to an organized list of the games! It should look like:

List: • Jailbreak • Adopt me ...etc..

(The list does put every single value on a seperate line,but StackOverflow doesn't want to show them properly for some reason)

Hope this helped! If it did,please mark my question as a valid answer.
